1.verbatim: Figure S1. Read accounting and reference recovery across the dataset. (A) For each lifestyle, the share of sequenced bases retained after trimming, host-read removal and alignment at MAPQ ≥30, against the combined reference; absolute totals and sample counts are printed beside each bar, and the pooled figure quoted in the main text is the bottom row. (B) The same quantity for each reference catalogue separately (Carter, 3,971 SGBs, 8.92 Gb; Leviatan, 3,594 SGBs, 8.75 Gb; combined, 5,081 SGBs, 11.62 Gb), each on its own analytic cohort; because a sample maps more bases against a larger catalogue, the per-sample floor retains slightly different samples per reference, but restricting all three to the 18,039 samples they share changes no rate by more than 0.03 percentage points. The dashed line is the chimpanzee catalogue over the 3,799 industrial samples processed against it that carry an archived sequencing total (Supplementary Text 4K), the floor a non-human catalogue reaches on these reads. The combined reference recovers more than either single catalogue in every lifestyle, and the Carter catalogue exceeds the Leviatan catalogue on hunter-gatherer samples (31.4% against 29.7%) while the two are level on industrial samples, the asymmetry in ascertainment their provenance predicts. (C) The per-sample distribution behind (A). The white marker is the group median and the bar its interquartile range; each point beside a violin is one study's median, for the 89 studies contributing at least ten samples. The difference is a property of studies rather than of samples: the median across 67 industrial studies is 0.444 against 0.361 across 22 non-industrial studies (Mann-Whitney on study medians, p = 4 × 10⁻⁶). (D) The same contrast within deciles of sequencing depth, equal in sample count. Industrial samples map a higher median fraction in all ten deciles, with a median gap of 9.3 percentage points, and mapped fraction is close to flat in depth within each group (Spearman ρ = +0.08 industrial, −0.01 non-industrial), so the difference is not the depth imbalance of Fig. S4 in another form. Mapped bases are Σ(mean depth × genome length) per sample and sequenced bases are the archived totals, so the unmapped remainder in (A) comprises trimmed, host-derived and unalignable reads together and is not attributable to catalogue coverage alone. The comparison in (B) holds reads, trimming and host removal fixed, and there the asymmetry is the catalogue's: non-industrial samples recover a smaller share against every human catalogue tested, and because an uncatalogued taxon contributes no mapped bases, the richness comparisons of Fig. 2 are made against a reference ascertainment bias that runs counter to them. 126 samples (0.7%) report fewer sequenced than mapped bases, an under-reported archive total, and carry no ratio in (C) and (D).

2.verbatim: Figure S2. Technical replicates confirm the high reproducibility of richness estimates, particularly in industrial samples. Scatter plots comparing SGB richness (≥10% breadth coverage) between primary and secondary sequencing runs from the same biosample (technical replicates), for Hunter-gatherer (orange, n=11), Agro-pastoralist (yellow, n=574), and Industrial (blue, n=2,761) samples. The dashed diagonal represents perfect concordance. Intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) are shown per group. Both groups appear to show instances of perfect sample replicates along the diagonal, and a more meaningful line showing secondary runs with lower richness (because we define the primary run as the run with the highest sequencing depth) that is strongly correlated to that of the primary run. Reads mapped to the Carter reference.

3.verbatim: Figure S3. Within-sample Bray-Curtis dissimilarity between technical replicates is low and largely independent of sequencing depth. Each point represents a pair of technical replicates (primary vs. secondary run, where primary runs were defined to have the higher sequencing depth) from the same individual, plotting the Bray-Curtis dissimilarity between the two runs (y-axis; 0 = identical composition, 1 = completely different) against the primary run's sequencing depth (log₁₀ total mapped bp; x-axis), for Hunter-gatherer (orange, n=11), Agro-pastoralist (yellow, n=574) and Industrial (blue, n=2,761) samples. The large majority of pairs cluster at near-zero dissimilarity, indicating that the compositional profiles of technical replicates are highly reproducible. A subset of pairs – particularly at intermediate sequencing depths (~10⁸·⁵–10⁹ bp) – show elevated dissimilarity (up to ~0.10). Reads mapped to the Carter reference.

4.verbatim: Figure S4. Sequencing depth distributions by lifestyle group, before depth-matching. Histograms of total bacterial bases mapped per sample (log₁₀ scale) for the three lifestyle groups present in the main dataset prior to any depth-matching: Hunter-gatherer (orange, n=401), Agro-pastoralist (yellow, n=3,697), and Industrial (blue, n=13,977). Dashed lines indicate group medians. Industrial samples are sequenced at substantially lower depth (median 1.7×10⁹ bp) than Agro-pastoralist (median 3.3×10⁹ bp) or Hunter-gatherer samples (median 6.1×10⁹ bp), reflecting systematic differences in sequencing effort across studies rather than biological differences. This confound motivates the depth-correction methods applied throughout the analysis.

5.verbatim: Figure S5. Read length has a minor but detectable effect on observed richness. (A-F) Per-sample richness (SGBs detected) as a function of sequencing depth (log₁₀ total mapped bp), with samples split into three read-length terciles: Short (≤99 bp, green), Medium (99–111 bp, orange), and Long (>111 bp, purple). Data are shown for all samples combined (A, D), Industrial samples only (B, E), and Non-Industrial samples only (C, F) . Longer reads detect modestly more taxa at equivalent sequencing depth. (G) Industrial and Agro-pastoralist samples are overwhelmingly sequenced with shorter reads (~100 bp) while H-G samples have longer reads (~150 bp median), creating a potential confound. (H) After controlling for sequencing depth, the residual association between read length and richness is small but statistically significant (Spearman ρ = −0.076, p = 4.6×10⁻¹³). However, because many samples sequenced with the longest reads were also sequenced with the greatest depth (e.g., Hadza and Nepali samples from Carter et al.), correction for sequencing depth cannot fully eliminate confounding due tostudy batch effects. (I) Predicted richness at 3 Gb sequencing depth by read-length tercile and lifestyle. Differences across terciles are modest relative to the between-lifestyle gap, indicating that read length is not a primary driver of the richness differences reported in the main text. Reads mapped to the Carter reference.

6.verbatim: Figure S6. Focus on samples from the Carter study: Geometric-mean-target weighting (GMW) corrects for sequencing depth bias in richness comparisons. Each row corresponds to a different taxon detection threshold (top: ≥10% breadth coverage; bottom: ≥200 kB mapped bases). Left panels show the sequencing depth density distributions for Industrial (blue) and Non-Industrial (agro-pastoralist + hunter-gatherer; gold) samples, with the GMW target distribution (black curve) overlaid. The GMW method reweights each sample in proportion to how well its depth matches this shared target, so that neither group is systematically favored. Middle panels show violin plots of raw (uncorrected) per-sample SGB richness; right panels show the GMW-corrected richness, with weighted means (white dots ± weighted SEM) and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The pattern here is similar to what we show in Fig. S10 below, albeit with a smaller effect size. GMW reweighting significantly reduces the apparent richness of non-industrial samples (by ~42 taxa). Reads mapped to the Carter reference.

7.verbatim: Figure S7. Focus on samples from the Carter study: Geometric-mean-target weighting (GMW) corrects for sequencing depth bias in richness comparisons between lifestyles. A 3-way comparison of GMW-corrected richness between Industrial, Agro-pastoralist, and Hunter-Gatherer samples in the Carter et al. sample set finds significantly smaller richness differences between Hunter-Gatherer and the other groups than without correction, and does not have sufficient power to detect any differences in richness between Industrial and Agro-pastoralist samples. The top row panels show the sequencing depth density distributions for Industrial (blue) and Non-Industrial (agro-pastoralist + hunter-gatherer; gold) samples, with the smoothed GMW target distribution (black curve) overlaid. The middle and bottom row show the results of applying this method to two different richness metrics: a coverage threshold where finding 10% or more of the SGB reference genome counts as a detection, and a flat threshold where finding 200kB or more of the SGB reference genome counts as a detection. The shadowed distribution is the raw distribution. Reweighting it substantially changes it for hunter-gatherers and somewhat shifts it for agro-pastoralist populations. Reads mapped to the Carter reference.

8.verbatim: Figure S8. Focus on samples from the Carter study: GMW-corrected richness gap between Industrial and non-Industrial samples is present at most detection thresholds. A 3-way comparison of GMW-corrected richness between Industrial, Agro-pastoralist, and Hunter-Gatherer samples in the Carter et al. sample set finds lower Industrial richness (75-95% of non-Industrial richness). This is systematically higher than the numbers reported in Fig. S13 (~55-80%) and may result from difference in sample selection in either the Carter study or our study. There might also be more instability in depth distribution smoothing (see Fig. S9) due to a sparser distribution of sample sequencing depth density (i.e., right-most panels show incomplete overlap between weighted distributions). Reads mapped to the Carter reference.

9.verbatim: Figure S9. Focus on samples from the Carter study: GMW weights as a function of sequencing depth. Curves show the Industrial and Non-Industrial depth distributions in the Carter-only subset together with the corresponding GMW weights across log10(mapped bp). Because the Carter-only subset is smaller and has sparser coverage of the depth range than the full dataset, the weights derived as a function of sequencing depth are noisier, especially in the tails where overlap is limited. This explains the slightly less stable Carter-only robustness estimates in Figs. S6–S8 without changing their qualitative interpretation: depth correction still reduces the apparent industrial versus non-industrial richness gap. Reads mapped to the Carter reference.

10.verbatim: Figure S10. Robustness of the industrial gut microbiota richness deficit across depth-correction methods and detection thresholds, based on SGBs mapped to the Carter reference database. (A) Sequencing depth distributions for Industrial (n = 13,977) and Non-Industrial (agro-pastoralist + hunter-gatherer; n = 4,098) samples, illustrating the ~1.7 Gb median depth imbalance that motivates depth correction. (B) Depth-stratified median richness (±IQR ribbon) for 1:1 depth-matched pairs (≥200 kB mapped bases; 3,282 pairs), showing that the richness gap between Industrial and Non-Industrial samples persists across the full range of sequencing depths. (C) Depth kernel density estimates and the geometric-mean-target distribution (√f̂~Ind~ · f̂~NI~, scaled) used to derive importance weights for our geometric-mean-target weighted (GMW) correction; effective sample sizes after weighting were ESS = 11,228/14,167 (Industrial) and 2,835/3,560 (Non-Industrial). (D–F) Per-sample richness distributions under uncorrected, 1:1 depth-matched, and GMW-corrected comparisons, respectively, using the ≥200 kB mapped-bases detection threshold. Richness ratios (Industrial/Non-Industrial median) were 0.53 (uncorrected, 95% CI [0.51, 0.54]), 0.75 ([0.73, 0.78]), and 0.73 ([0.71, 0.74]). (G–I) Equivalent comparisons using the ≥10% breadth coverage threshold, yielding ratios of 0.50 ([0.48, 0.51]), 0.73 ([0.70, 0.75]), and 0.70 ([0.68, 0.71]). (J) Forest plot summarizing all six method × threshold combinations. After depth correction, richness ratios converged to a consistent range of 0.70–0.75 regardless of correction method or detection threshold, in contrast to the uncorrected ratios of 0.50–0.53, which reflect differences in sequencing depth rather than true biological difference. The robustness of the corrected estimates across two independent methods (1:1 matching and GMW reweighting) and two detection thresholds supports the reliability of the reported richness deficit. See Supplementary Text #3 for GMW method details. Reads mapped to the Carter reference.

11.verbatim: Figure S11. Geometric-mean-target weighting (GMW) corrects for sequencing depth bias in richness comparisons. Each row corresponds to a different taxon detection threshold (top: ≥10% breadth coverage; bottom: ≥200 kB mapped bases). Left panels show the sequencing depth density distributions for Industrial (blue) and Non-Industrial (agro-pastoralist + hunter-gatherer; gold) samples, with the smoothed GMW target distribution (black curve) overlaid. The GMW method reweights each sample in proportion to how well its depth matches this shared target, so that neither group is systematically favoured. Middle panels show violin plots of raw (uncorrected) per-sample SGB richness; right panels show the GMW-corrected richness, with weighted means (white dots ± weighted SEM) and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. Before correction, Industrial samples appear to harbour only ~44–47% of Non-Industrial richness; after depth correction, this narrows to ~63–66%, indicating that a substantial but not complete portion of the apparent richness gap was driven by the lower sequencing depth of industrial samples. ESS = effective sample size after reweighting. Reads mapped to the Carter reference.

12.verbatim: Figure S12. 3x2-way comparison of geometric-mean-target weighting (GMW) corrects for sequencing depth bias in richness comparisons among Hunter-Gatherers (H-G), Agro-pastoralist, and Industrial (Ind) populations. Left panels show the sequencing depth density distributions for Industrial (blue), Agro-pastoralist (yellow) samples, with the smoothed GMW target distribution (black curve) overlaid. 13.verbatim: Figure S13. 3-way comparison of geometric-mean-target weighting (GMW) corrects for sequencing depth bias in richness comparisons between Hunter-Gatherers (H-G), Agro-pastoralist, and Healthy Industrial (IndH) populations. 14.verbatim: Figure S14. GMW-corrected richness gap is robust across all detection thresholds. Forest plot showing the absolute (left) and relative (right) richness difference between Industrial and Non-Industrial samples across twelve taxon-detection thresholds: six breadth-coverage cutoffs (1–90% of the genome covered) and six flat minimum-mapped-base cutoffs (10 kB–1 Mb). Grey diamonds show the raw (uncorrected) difference; orange and blue circles with 95% bootstrap confidence intervals show the GMW depth-corrected estimates. Across all thresholds, the corrected estimates are consistently less negative than the raw values. This confirms that lower sequencing depth in industrial samples inflates the apparent richness gap. Even so, all corrected estimates remain substantially negative, with richness in Industrial populations being 20–45% below richness in Non-Industrial populations, depending on threshold). Reads mapped to the Carter reference.

15.verbatim: Figure S15. Extensive microbial extinction has not occurred in industrial populations (empirical Hill-type Michaelis-Menten fit). Left panels: Expected number of SGBs detected as a function of number of pooled samples. Right panels: Expected number of SGBs detected as a function of number of pooled studies. Outer plots are shown in linear space; inner insets are shown in log-linear space. Curves show the bootstrap mean with 95% quantile ribbons; the fitted line [3-parameter Hill-type Michaelis-Menten] is shown within the observed range. Asymptote annotations give the fitted convergence value (median) with 95% bootstrap CI. (A, B) Data for SGB accumulation using the Carter reference (Hadza + UHGG) biased towards non-industrial samples. (C, D) Data for SGB accumulation using the Leviatan reference biased towards industrial samples. 18.verbatim: Figure S18. Coordinate-invariant projection of Agro-pastoralist populations into Hunter-Gatherer→Industrial axis space, aggregated by lifestyle and reported by sequencing depth bin. The study centroid is shown for all matched samples projected onto a normalized axis whose endpoints are the Hunter-Gatherer and Industrial centroids within the corresponding depth bin. The x-axis gives the sample’s fractional position along this Hunter-Gatherer→Industrial axis (0 = Hunter-Gatherer centroid, 1 = Industrial centroid), while the y-axis gives signed off-axis displacement, oriented so that positive values lie on the Agro-pastoralist side. Agro-pastoralist samples are intermediate along the main Hunter-Gatherer→Industrial axis but remain consistently displaced off that axis regardless of bin considered, indicating that the shift into agro-pastoralist microbiome composition is not collinear with the direct Hunter-Gatherer→Industrial contrast. The displacement to the Hunter-Gatherer→Industrial axis is consistent with sequencing depth. Reads mapped to the Carter reference.

19.verbatim: Figure S19. Coordinate-invariant projection of samples matched in 17 separate depth bins (see Fig. S18) into Hunter-Gatherer→Industrial axis space, aggregated by study. The study centroid is shown for all matched samples projected onto a normalized axis whose endpoints are the Hunter-Gatherer and Industrial centroids within the corresponding depth bin. Agro-pastoralist samples are intermediate along the main Hunter-Gatherer→Industrial axis but remain consistently displaced off that axis, indicating that the shift into agro-pastoralist microbiome composition is not collinear with the direct Hunter-Gatherer→Industrial contrast. A few populations are clearly borderline between the two categories (e.g. PehrrsonEC (El Salvador, Peru), VangayP (Thailand), and TamburiniFB (South Africa). These populations consist of peri-urban populations in developing countries that are likely not fully “industrialized”. We note that they are not sequenced particularly deeply and broadly and we do not expect them to lead to substantial misindentification of SGBs in our accumulation analysis.

20.verbatim: Figure S20. Depth-controlled richness variability within lifestyle groups. Samples were assigned species presence using the ≥10% breadth coverage threshold and binned into 40 equally log-spaced sequencing depth bins (x-axis; Gbp mapped). Left panel: median richness per bin by lifestyle, with ribbon showing the interquartile range; the positive depth–richness relationship is consistent across all three lifestyles (Spearman ρ = 0.80, 0.68, and 0.65 for H-G, Agro-pastoralist, and Industrial, respectively). Right panel: coefficient of variation (CV = SD/median richness) per occupied bin (minimum 10 samples per bin), colored separately by lifestyle. Grand mean CV differed significantly across lifestyles (H-G = 0.27 across 13 qualifying bins, Agro-pastoralist = 0.40 across 26 bins, Industrial = 0.45 across 33 bins; Kruskal–Wallis H = 29.66, p = 3.6 × 10⁻⁷; permutation test on maximum pairwise mean-CV difference: observed Δ = 0.18, p = 0.0002), with all pairwise comparisons significant after Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) correction (H-G vs. Agro-pastoralist: pBH = 2.8 × 10⁻⁴, r = 0.75; H-G vs. Industrial: pBH = 3.6 × 10⁻⁶, r = 0.93; Agro-pastoralist vs. Industrial: pBH = 0.003, r = 0.45). The lower CV in H-G samples likely reflects the smaller number of contributing studies and the narrower geographic range of sampled hunter-gatherer populations, rather than lower true biological variability. Crucially, CV values of 0.27–0.45 persist across the full depth range in all three lifestyle groups, confirming that substantial richness variation remains after controlling for sequencing depth and is not a depth artefact. Reads mapped to the Carter reference.

21.verbatim: Figure S21. Pairwise overlap among original (VANISH/BloSSUM), industrialization-defined (VANISH+, BloSSUM+), and H+-restricted (VANISHH+, BloSSUMH+) taxon lists. The figure summarizes overlap within each family (VANISH on the left; BloSSUM on the right) between the original Carter lists, our “+” lists defined from the industrial versus non-industrial comparison in the present dataset, and our “H+” lists defined from the non-industrial versus healthy-industrial comparison in the present dataset. Labels report list sizes and pairwise overlap, and the Jaccard index quantifies similarity as |A∩B| / |A∪B|. High overlap between the + and H+ lists indicates continuity within each family, whereas the more modest overlap between the original and +/H+ lists shows that these new lists capture related but non-identical aspects of lifestyle-associated prevalence structure.

22.verbatim: Figure S22. Breakdown of VANISH/BloSSUM and VANISH+/BloSSUM+ taxa detection by continent and lifestyle. Most categories recover most of the taxa. The exceptions are the categories with low sequencing depth (e.g. hunter-gatherers in South America). Because these cohorts are not balanced or corrected for sequencing depth, so cross-interpretation is not intended between cohorts, only within cohorts. 24.verbatim: Figure S24. 3x2-way comparison of geometric-mean-target weighting (GMW) corrects for sequencing depth bias in richness comparisons between Non-Industrial, Healthy Industrial, and Unhealthy Industrial populations. Each row corresponds to a comparison within a pair of lifestyle groups. Left panels show the sequencing depth density distributions for Industrial Healthy (dark green), Industrial Unhealthy (dark blue) and non-Industrial (gold) samples, with the smoothed GMW target distribution (black curve) overlaid. The GMW method reweights each sample in proportion to how well its depth matches this shared target, so that neither group is systematically favoured. Middle panels show violin plots of raw (uncorrected) per-sample SGB richness; right panels show the GMW-corrected richness, with weighted means (white dots ± weighted SEM) and 95% bootstrap confidence intervals. The results are slightly different to those displayed in Figure 5A-C in the main text, where the reweighting target is chosen as the geometric mean of all 3 lifestyle groups simultaneously, rather than for each of the pairwise comparisons shown here.

25.verbatim: Figure S25. The prevalence background, original VANISH and BloSSUM lists. For each of the five reported conditions, every background taxon's study-stratified case−control prevalence difference is plotted against its control prevalence (grey points), with the fitted background curve and its ±1 SD band. List taxa are drawn on top: VANISH in orange (upper row) and BloSSUM in blue (lower row). Each panel prints the list's mean distance from the curve in units of the local spread, with a bootstrap 95% interval that refits the curve on resampled background taxa, and stars from the two-sided bootstrap p-value under the 10% breadth rule. Taxa with fewer than 15 comparable background taxa within 0.25 log10 of their control prevalence are plotted but excluded from the mean. The curve turns down at high prevalence because a taxon present in almost every control has room to fall and none to rise; the question each panel asks is whether the list sits above or below that expectation rather than above or below zero. Main-text Figure 5E is the same figure for the VANISHH+ and BloSSUMH+ lists.

26.verbatim: Figure S26. Taxa contributing most to the VANISHH+ health association. Each VANISHH+ taxon is scored, separately in each of the five reported conditions, by its distance from the fitted prevalence background in units of the local spread (z; Supplementary Text #6E–6F); the mean of those values over the taxa of a list is the list-level statistic plotted in Fig. 5E, so this figure decomposes that number. A taxon is eligible when it is scored in at least three conditions and shifts in the same direction in at least 70% of them; 70 VANISHH+ taxa are eligible, 36 lying above the background and 34 below. The figure draws the 16 that are individually significant at an uncorrected p < 0.05, nine above the background and seven below. Left: z per taxon and condition — blue where a taxon is less depleted in cases than taxa of the same baseline prevalence, orange where it is more depleted, grey where the taxon was not scored in that condition. Centre: each taxon’s driver score, the mean of its per-condition z values, with a 95% confidence interval from the t-distribution on those values; stars are the uncorrected one-sample t-test (*p < 0.05, **p < 0.01, ***p < 0.001), which is also the selection criterion, so every drawn interval is clear of zero. Right: directional consistency against driver score, with point size and opacity scaled by −log10(q), the Benjamini–Hochberg value within the list; 12 of the 16 drawn taxa also reach q < 0.20. The enriched side is led by Escherichia coli (+2.42), Fimenecus sp000432435 (+1.93) and Prevotella copri_N (+1.52); the depleted side by Faecalibacterium prausnitzii_E (−1.18), Eshraghiella crossota (−1.08) and Prevotella caccae (−0.78). Prevotella appears on both sides — four species above the background and two below — so the list is not uniformly directional at the taxon level, consistent with the condition-specific list-level result in Fig. 5E.

27.verbatim: Figure S27. Taxa contributing most to the BloSSUMH+ health association. Layout, scoring and selection are as in Fig. S26, applied to the BloSSUMH+ list. Of the 72 eligible BloSSUMH+ taxa, 62 lie above the fitted prevalence background and 10 below; 29 are individually significant at an uncorrected p < 0.05, and all 29 lie above the background — no BloSSUMH+ taxon is significantly more depleted in cases than its prevalence-matched comparators. The strongest drivers are Mediterraneibacter gnavus (+3.38), Flavonifractor plautii (+3.01), M. torques (+2.58), Bacteroides fragilis (+2.54) and Eggerthella lenta (+2.49); the set runs through Bacteroides, Alistipes, Oscillibacter, Lawsonibacter and Parabacteroides species to Coprobacter fastidiosus (+0.48). Taxa enriched by industrialization therefore move with disease status in one direction at the taxon level as well as in aggregate, matching the list-level result in which BloSSUMH+ stands above its background in four of the five tested conditions (Fig. 5E).

28.verbatim: Figure S28. Taxa contributing most to the original VANISH health association. Layout, scoring and selection are as in Fig. S26, applied to the original VANISH list. Fifty-five VANISH taxa are eligible, 27 lying above the fitted prevalence background and 28 below — the only one of the four lists that is not weighted toward the enriched side. Ten are individually significant at an uncorrected p < 0.05, and these too split against the enriched direction, three above the background and seven below. Only three of the ten also reach q < 0.20 within the list, so the depleted drivers in particular should be read as candidates rather than as established associations. Above the background: Prevotella sp900548745 (+1.07), Cryptobacteroides sp934700615 (+0.69) and Sarcina ventriculi (+0.67). Below it: Holdemanella sp934754935 (−0.80), Minthosoma sp934293005 (−0.72), Oscillibacter sp900550685 (−0.71), Phascolarctobacterium_A sp022718015 (−0.69), Ventricola sp. (−0.67), Anaerobutyricum sp934317185 (−0.63) and Cryptobacteroides sp900546445 (−0.48); five of these are scored in only three of the five conditions, shown grey in the heatmap. Taxa detected in no sample of either arm are excluded throughout: their case–control shift is zero because nothing was observed rather than because nothing moved, and all of them would otherwise receive the same score at the prevalence floor.

(−0.67), Anaerobutyricum sp934317185 (−0.63) and Cryptobacteroides sp900546445 (−0.48); five of these are scored in only three of the five conditions, shown grey in the heatmap. Taxa detected in no sample of either arm are excluded throughout: their case–control shift is zero because nothing was observed rather than because nothing moved, and all of them would otherwise receive the same score at the prevalence floor.

29.verbatim: Figure S29. Taxa contributing most to the original BloSSUM health association. Layout, scoring and selection are as in Fig. S26, applied to the original BloSSUM list. Forty-one BloSSUM taxa are eligible, 37 lying above the fitted prevalence background and 4 below; 17 are individually significant at an uncorrected p < 0.05, 14 above the background and 3 below, and all 17 also reach q < 0.20 within the list. The enriched side is led by Mediterraneibacter torques (+2.58), Bacteroides thetaiotaomicron (+1.94), B. stercoris (+1.76) and Oscillibacter welbionis (+1.75), and includes both Sutterella wadsworthensis clades, Alistipes putredinis and Megamonas funiformis; below the background are Dialister hominis (−0.89), Bifidobacterium catenulatum (−0.57) and Mediterraneibacter lactaris (−0.45). 30.verbatim: Figure S30. Within one genus or family, list members behave differently from their relatives. Each panel takes one disease condition and one clade, and compares the distance from the prevalence background of the clade's list members (coloured) against every other catalogue taxon in the same clade (grey); higher values mean a taxon is less depleted in cases than its baseline prevalence predicts. The background curve is refitted with the clade excluded before scoring, so a large clade is not partly its own control, and only clades with at least five catalogue taxa are tested. Horizontal bars mark group means, and each panel prints the difference between them in SD units with its permutation p and Benjamini–Hochberg q across clades; the three most extreme list members are named. The six panels shown are those surviving correction and spanning both list families: Prevotella under obesity and Oscillospiraceae under IBD for VANISHH+, Lachnospiraceae under the unhealthy and IBD contrasts for BloSSUM+, and Oscillospiraceae and Bacteroides for BloSSUMH+. Oscillospiraceae under IBD is the one panel in which the list members sit below their relatives; in the other five they sit above, so the list-level signal is not an artefact of the clades those lists happen to contain.
